system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2136-01-17 01:02:00 to 2136-01-21 15:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of tracheostomy, prior cerebrovascular accident with nonverbal and immobile baseline, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, and recurrent infections was admitted from a nursing home for decreased responsiveness and hypotension. He was found to be in septic shock with evidence of urosepsis, supported by purulent urine and growth of Proteus mirabilis in urine culture, though pneumonia was also considered due to new lung opacities on imaging. He was treated with fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem and vancomycin), and close monitoring. A PICC line was placed for outpatient antibiotic completion. His renal function improved, and he regained baseline mental responsiveness by discharge. Code status was updated to DNR with allowance for trach ventilation. He was discharged to extended care with plans to complete a 5-day course of IV antibiotics, monitor vancomycin levels, and hold warfarin until INR normalized.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Late effects of cerebrovascular disease, other speech and language deficits

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  A ___ man with CVA and clogged ___ tube.  Please unclog
the ___ tube.

RADIOLOGISTS:  Dr. ___ performed the procedure (fellow).  Dr.
___ (attending physician) reviewed the images, was present and supervised
throughout the procedure.

ANESTHESIA: Local anesthesia was provided with lidocaine gel.

PROCEDURE: Telephone consent was obtained from the patient's son after
explaining the procedure, risks, benefits, and alternatives to it.  The
patient was brought to the angiographic suite and laid supine on the table. 
The indwelling ___ tube was prepped and draped in a sterile fashion.  A
preprocedural huddle and timeout were performed per ___ protocol.

An initial scout image demonstrated the presence of the existing ___ tube in
the expected position.  Initial flush with normal saline was unsuccessful.  A
super-stiff Glidewire was then advanced through the ___ tube up to about 3 cm
from the tip.  The wire was then taken out and then another was flush with
saline cleared the tube.  The super-stiff Glidewire was reintroduced and
coiled in the duodenum.  A Kumpe was then introduced to guide the wire down
into the jejunum.  Once the wire was in the jejunum, the Kumpe was exchanged
for another 14 ___ ___ tube with the tip in the jejunum.  The pig
tail of the ___ tube was left just beyond the pylorus.  The placement was
confirmed by contrast injection.  Free flow of contrast was demonstrated
through the small bowel.

The loop was tightened and secured.  Sterile dressings were applied to the
tube.  All wires were removed.  The patient tolerated the procedure well. 
There were no immediate complications.

IMPRESSION:  Successful exchange of a clogged 14 ___ ___ tube with a
similar tube.  The tip of the catheter is in the jejunum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. I know you can’t speak, but if you understand me, could you please nod your head?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods slowly*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. We brought you in because your nursing home said your belly was getting bigger and you seemed uncomfortable. You also had a fever. Do you feel pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *shakes head no*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. In the ER, we found your catheter was blocked. We replaced it and drained 800cc of cloudy urine. That’s likely why your belly was swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started you on an antibiotic called cefepime through your IV to treat a possible urinary infection. We’re also giving fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work shows your white count was high last night—18.9—so we’re definitely dealing with an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray doesn’t show pneumonia, so we think the infection is coming from your bladder. The urine culture is pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods slowly*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just got a preliminary result: gram-negative rods in your urine. That supports a urinary infection. We’ll keep you on IV antibiotics for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down—now 7.6. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: But you mentioned leg pain yesterday. Can you point to where it hurts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *moves eyes toward right leg*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Your right foot was cool and we couldn’t find a pulse at first. But this morning, it’s warmer and we can feel a faint pulse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vascular surgery saw you. They think it was vasospasm, not a clot. Since you’re on blood thinners and the pulse returned, they don’t recommend surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep giving pain medicine—morphine and your fentanyl patch. Let us know if it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture is back. It grew Proteus, Klebsiella, and Morganella—all sensitive to ceftriaxone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching your antibiotic from cefepime to ceftriaxone. It’s simpler and targets the exact bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get IV ceftriaxone once a day for 7 more days after discharge. We’ll set up home health for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your G-tube got clogged yesterday. The radiology team helped unclog it using a wire and contrast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They confirmed the tube is now working and in the right place—into your jejunum. We’ll flush it regularly to prevent this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sacral wound is looking better. The wound care team applied Duoderm and said it’s healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your INR today—it’s 2.8. That means your warfarin is in a safe range. We lowered your dose to 4mg daily from 4.5mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home on 4mg. Your nursing home will continue your other meds like insulin, thyroid pill, and mirtazapine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. No fever, white count is normal, and your leg is warm with a detectable pulse. We’re planning to discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods with slight smile*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your G-tube and catheter are secure. You’ll finish the ceftriaxone at the facility with visiting nurses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I spoke with your nursing home. They’ll restart your regular morphine for pain as needed, every 6 hours via G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we’re restarting your furosemide for blood pressure. Same dose as before, 20mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your Cymbalta was held because it can’t be crushed. But we’ll restart it at the facility since it can go through the G-tube whole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. Your infection is clearing, leg pain is gone, and all your tubes are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods slowly*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get ceftriaxone IV once a day for 7 more days. The nurse will come to your facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your other meds as before. If your leg gets cold or painful again, let the nurses know right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods firmly*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fentanyl patch is being increased to 75 mcg/hr. We’ll monitor for comfort. Any breathing issues, let us know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with urology soon. They’ll check your catheter and bladder health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send all instructions to your nursing home. You did really well. Get some rest when you get back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *gives weak thumbs up*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—your pain is under control now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your breathing? Any shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *shakes head no*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your oxygen levels are stable. We’ll keep your trach mask as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is here. They’ll take you back safely. We’ll call the facility to confirm everything’s set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for being so cooperative. Take care, and we’re always here if the facility needs us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *gives small wave*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in before you leave—any last questions or concerns?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *shakes head no*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If anything changes—fever, pain, swelling—your team will know what to do. You’re in good hands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods with eyes closed*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. All set for the ride back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: *nods*

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll be checking in with your facility. Rest well.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male nursing home resident with a history of cerebrovascular accident, tracheostomy, G-tube, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, diabetes, and recurrent urinary infections was admitted for suprapubic tenderness, abdominal distention, and fever. In the ER, his Foley catheter was found blocked and replaced, draining 800cc of cloudy urine. He was started on IV cefepime for suspected urosepsis. Blood cultures were negative, but urine culture grew Proteus, Klebsiella, and Morganella, all sensitive to ceftriaxone, prompting a switch in antibiotics. He developed right leg pain with a cool foot and absent pulse, initially concerning for ischemia, but vascular surgery attributed it to vasospasm given improvement and ongoing anticoagulation. The foot rewarmed and pulse returned. His G-tube became clogged and was successfully cleared by interventional radiology. His infection resolved, pain was controlled, and he was discharged to extended care on a 7-day course of IV ceftriaxone, with all home medications resumed including warfarin at 4mg daily.
